prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate economic fluctuations, providing the theory of credit cycles

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) provide a tractable dynamic general-equilibrium mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to the value of collateral assets create a feedback loop between asset prices and credit. Small or temporary shocks then become large and persistent, and the model explains why. The mechanism is conceptually foundational and has been absorbed into quantitative macro, macro-finance and central-bank models. It was extended widely after 2008, so there is nearly three decades of theoretical, quantitative and policy follow-up. It also serves as a building block for the heterogeneous-agent and financial-friction models I know best. In my reading, scientific merit, attribution clarity and maturity all point the same way. The original paper has two authors, and the contribution does not depend on a contested credit split.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig on banks and financial crises, which the Committee could regard as having covered this territory. The empirical identification of collateral-driven amplification is also less clean than the theory, and the quantitative size of the amplification is debated. The theory is highly influential, but the case that it is a distinct discovery rests on the collateral and asset-price mechanism being separable from bank runs and intermediation. That separation is a judgment, not a settled fact.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore. The accelerator was already central to the 2022 prize through Bernanke, so adding Gertler or Gilchrist blurs the lines of credit.
responses.response: This persuades me to narrow my own opening proposal. I originally included Gertler, but the argument that the clean, originating contribution is the two-author collateral-constraint model is stronger than I gave it credit for. I still think Gertler's work is substantive. I now judge that including him ties the citation to a strand partly covered by the 2022 recognition, and it weakens the separation I rely on above. I concede this and have dropped him from my preferred configuration.

responses.point: Strömberg argues that, since Bernanke is already a laureate, Gertler is the natural remaining name from the accelerator lineage. Strömberg also notes that Gertler appears in the New Keynesian ballot, so credit may be split.
responses.response: I take the second point seriously, because it is a real attribution problem. Gertler's credit is spread across B002 and B043, and a laureate is best chosen for a clearly bounded contribution. I disagree with the first point. The accelerator lineage has two other originators, one of whom is already recognised, so adding Gertler would reward a co-contributor to a strand and could leave Gilchrist as an obvious omission. I would revisit his inclusion only if the Committee decides the citation should explicitly cover financial frictions in monetary transmission, which is a different and broader prize.

responses.point: Friberg ranks heterogeneous-firm trade (B025) first. He sees a very high-originality framework that reorganised trade, with more than twenty years of confirmation, and Melitz and Helpman as the cleanest pairing.
responses.response: I agree B025 is mature and well attributed, and I kept it as an alternative for that reason. Our difference is mainly one of weighing. I see the Krugman 2008 prize as a closer neighbour than Friberg does, and I think the contribution is more a shift in the unit of analysis than a new causal mechanism. Friberg's own opening notes the concern about related work by Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not credited. I do not regard that as disqualifying, but it makes the Helpman-Melitz attribution less clean than the two-author Kiyotaki-Moore case.

responses.point: Andersson ranks structural demand and industry estimation (B012) first. He values the methodological reach of BLP and Ericson-Pakes, and the maturity is not in doubt. He also flags that a three-name limit omits real contributors.
responses.response: I agree on the reach and maturity of the BLP core, and I rank it in my top four. Andersson's own caveat is one I share. Bresnahan and others are foundational for empirical IO, so a three-person BLP prize risks a citation that looks narrower than the field it represents. I am also wary of letting a method's wide use substitute for a discovery. That is a judgment I hold lightly, since Andersson's view that this methodology made a field quantitative is reasonable. I treat B012 as a serious alternative and not as my first choice.

uncertainties: How much of the credit-cycle mechanism the Committee views as already covered by the 2022 banking and financial-crisis prize.
Whether leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist makes the citation look incomplete relative to the financial-accelerator literature. I have not independently verified how that literature divides credit.
How strongly the empirical evidence supports quantitatively large collateral amplification.
Whether B025 or B012 would, on a fuller attribution review, be the stronger alternative if the 2022 overlap proves decisive.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent with the B002 candidates from the supplied profile. Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler and Gilchrist are not listed among my co-authors. I disclose long-term co-authorship with John Hassler (chair) and Timo Boppart (co-opted member), who are colleagues and not candidates. Several other profile co-authors, such as Violante, Ríos-Rull and Smith, are not on the shortlist. My research is in heterogeneous-agent and quantitative macro, which is adjacent to macro-finance, and I do not treat that as a conflict.
